clue.text: Guaranteed essentially filling food from part of Scandinavia

indicators.note: the two central letters go inside, filling the word for food

parts.note: a dish is a prepared serving of food

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only its middle letters are used

explanation.surface: Something about a reliable dish from Scandinavia, as if recommending a guaranteed Nordic meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'food' looks like the definition but is the container; the definition is the adjective 'from part of Scandinavia'. 'essentially' and 'filling' are the indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: Denmark is one of the Scandinavian countries, so its adjective describes something coming from that part of the region.

clue.text: Time of year car park is regularly close to full

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken
the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A car park filling up almost to capacity at a certain season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of CAR PARK IS, APRI, and 'close to' adds L from 'full'.
explanation.definitionFit: A month is a period of the calendar, here the fourth one, in spring.

clue.text: Foolishly Dominican's beginning to ignore suffering from sleeplessness

indicators.note: foolishly means done in a silly, disordered way, so the letters are jumbled
the beginning of the word is ignored, dropping its first letter

explanation.surface: A Dominican friar who has begun to neglect himself suffers from lack of sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to ignore' drops the D from DOMINICANS, and 'Foolishly' rearranges OMINICANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, the word describes a person who habitually cannot get to sleep.

clue.text: Attractive individual getting hot for large rugby player

indicators.note: getting one letter in place of another signals a swap
for here means in place of, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: a looker is a good-looking person
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A handsome man swaps warmth for size to play rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap L for H in LOOKER. In rugby union the hooker is the front-row forward who hooks the ball back in a scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A forward in the middle of a rugby scrum's front row, named for heeling the ball back.

clue.text: Refuse to accept former company representative having authority

indicators.note: the word for refuse takes in, or accepts, the company's initials

parts.note: offal is waste parts, refuse from a butchered animal
ICI, Imperial Chemical Industries, was a major British firm, now gone

explanation.surface: Someone declining to take on an ex-employee as an authorised agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as the verb but is the noun, rubbish: OFFAL. ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, a large British chemicals company taken over in 2008.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun meaning a person holding office with power to act, such as a referee or civil servant.

clue.text: Novel is one well-known to each of us

definitions.meaning: the title of a book by Charles Dickens, his last finished novel

definitions.text: one well-known to each of us
definitions.meaning: a person both of us know, paraphrased into the title's words

explanation.surface: A book is something everyone among us knows well.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's 1865 novel has a title that is itself an everyday phrase for a shared acquaintance.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens wrote the 1865 novel of this name; the phrase also means a person known to both speakers.

clue.text: Ineffectiveness of fine against public service

indicators.note: against means up against, next to, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil grades
a utility is a public service such as gas, water or electricity

explanation.surface: Questioning how useless a fine is against a public-service company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'against' places F alongside UTILITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Pointlessness, the state of achieving nothing, is the lack of any useful result or effect.

clue.text: Variety of pear detailed in illustrated magazine

indicators.note: de-tailed means having its tail, the last letter, cut off

parts.note: the Comice is a variety of dessert pear

explanation.surface: A sort of pear pictured in detail in a glossy magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as 'thorough' but means de-tailed: COMICE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's paper or book of picture strips, like the Beano, is a magazine told in drawings.

clue.text: Gathered embarrassment visiting island upset daughter

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so read in reverse
visiting means calling in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island of Napoleon's exile
a mess is an awkward or embarrassing predicament

explanation.surface: A daughter upset by an embarrassing trip to an island has gathered herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'visiting' and 'upset' work in turn: the insertion comes first, then the whole is read upwards, as 'upset' suits a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: When people have gathered, they have come together in one place as a group.

clue.text: Noble actor is about to get into painting

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are put inside the word for painting

parts.note: painting is a form of art

indicators.note: about here means scrambled around, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: An actor taking up painting, the idea of a performer turning to art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' but is the anagram signal; 'to get into' then does the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A noble is a member of the titled upper class, the same rank as a peer or lord.

clue.text: Film failed to be broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means spoken over the air, so the word is taken as heard

parts.note: to have failed to hit is to have missed

explanation.surface: A film that flopped and never made it to television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like a movie but means a thin layer, as of haze on glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin film of condensed vapour on a window or a lens is a light haze of droplets.

clue.text: Boyfriend joins family across capital, ultimately to see Olympic Torch?

indicators.note: joins places one piece next to another
the family word stretches across, enclosing, the final letter

parts.note: FAM is a short form of family

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter is taken

parts.note: a beau is an old word for a boyfriend or suitor

explanation.surface: A couple and relatives travel to a capital city to watch the Olympic flame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes L from 'capital', and 'across' puts FAM around it to make FLAM. The question mark flags a definition by example: an Olympic torch is one instance.
explanation.definitionFit: A flaming torch carried in procession, as the Olympic flame is, is the classic example of this kind of light.

clue.text: Substitutes Greek character blocking second pass back

indicators.note: back means the whole result is read in the reverse direction
the Greek letter sits between the two other pieces, blocking the way

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A Greek player stops a second pass going backwards, a football scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pass' suggests football but is a mountain col. 'blocking' does the insertion and 'back' reverses everything, giving SMUCOL read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Stand-ins who cover for an absent doctor or pharmacist are temporary replacements in the job.

clue.text: Shop of fine appearance? Not half

indicators.note: without its second half, only the first half of the word remains

parts.note: delicate means fine and dainty in appearance

explanation.surface: A shop that looks rather good, asked as a question with a slangy reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is British slang for 'very much', but here it drops half of DELICATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A short form of delicatessen, a store selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared food.

clue.text: Condense mostly impressive book describing centre of Bratislava

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: epic means grand and impressive

indicators.note: describing means drawing a line around, so the book word encloses the middle

parts.note: a tome is a large book

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters

explanation.surface: Someone asked to sum up an impressive book about the Slovak capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' means drawing round, not portraying. 'mostly' and 'centre of' are the other indicators; Bratislava is the Slovak capital.
explanation.definitionFit: To condense something into a perfect short example is to embody or encapsulate it.

clue.text: BBC loses case most originally see as inopportune

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer letters, which are dropped

parts.note: Auntie is a British nickname for the BBC

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so the first letter is taken

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city, and a see is a bishop's seat

explanation.surface: The BBC losing a court case is viewed as badly timed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auntie' is a fond British nickname for the BBC; 'loses case' strips its A and E to give UNTI. 'originally' takes M from 'most'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something badly timed, coming at the wrong moment, is premature or ill-suited to the occasion.

clue.text: Drain cash fund to obtain electric vehicle

parts.note: to milk is to drain or exploit
a float is a sum of cash kept for giving change

explanation.surface: Draining a pot of money to buy an electric car.
explanation.walkthrough: A milk float is the small battery-powered van British milkmen used for doorstep deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: A battery-driven British delivery van once used to bring milk to people's doors.

clue.text: Spendthrift pair with gold becoming spoilt

indicators.note: spoilt means damaged out of its proper form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wasteful couple with their gold turn into spoilt brats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoilt' rearranges PAIR and GOLD together.
explanation.definitionFit: A wasteful person who squanders money, as in the parable of the son who blew his inheritance.

clue.text: Instinctive swimming rivals, extremely competitive at heart

indicators.note: the outer letters go into the centre of the rearranged word
swimming suggests movement, so the letters are moved about
extremely means at the extremes, so the first and last letters are used

explanation.surface: Swimmers racing each other with a fiercely competitive spirit at their core.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' turns RIVALS into VISRAL, and 'at heart' puts CE (the ends of 'competitive') in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A gut reaction comes from deep feeling rather than reason, which is what an instinctive response is.

clue.text: Woman's complaint when mother leaves

indicators.note: leaves means goes away, so these letters are removed

parts.note: a malady is an illness or complaint
ma is a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: A woman's grumble as her mother walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complaint' reads as a grievance but means an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: A polite term for a female adult, as in the ladies and gentlemen of an audience.

clue.text: Compete over news article that generates capital

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above what follows

parts.note: to vie is to compete
N is the abbreviation for new, and the plural gives two of them
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Rivals fight over a news story that brings in money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is read as new plural, giving two Ns. 'capital' looks like money but is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The city on the Danube is the seat of government of Austria.

clue.text: Deny purpose of attending auction?

definitions.meaning: to deny here is to prohibit or refuse permission
split three and three, it says you went in order to make an offer

explanation.surface: Refusing to say why you went to a sale.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into two words: going somewhere 'for' the chance to put in an offer.
explanation.definitionFit: To deny someone something can mean to refuse to allow it, the same as prohibiting it.

clue.text: Graduate taking the plunge?

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate's degree

explanation.surface: A new graduate taking a big step into the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking the plunge' usually means committing to something big; here it is a literal dip in water.
explanation.definitionFit: To go swimming, taking a dip, is to plunge into water.

clue.text: At home, slip by artist in shower

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist
in means at home
to slip is to fall

explanation.surface: Someone at home slips beside a painter in the shower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shower' looks like the bathroom fixture but is a brief spell of rain.
explanation.definitionFit: A shower is a brief downpour, and the amount of water coming from the sky is measured as this.

clue.text: Defeated player looks teary from time to time

indicators.note: from time to time means now and then, so alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: A beaten player who looks on the verge of tears every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from time to time' takes the odd letters of LOOKS TEARY.
explanation.definitionFit: The one who has lost a contest or game, the opposite of the winner.

clue.text: Natural talent is something easily understood

definitions.meaning: an inborn knack or aptitude for something
informally, a thing so easy it is handed to you, like a question that answers itself

explanation.surface: A natural talent is something easily understood.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural flair is said to be given at birth; an easy task or question is likewise called a present or freebie.

clue.text: Cutting temperatures toughens tree out in conservatory

indicators.note: cutting means removing letters from the words that follow
out means put out of order, so the remaining letters are rearranged

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature, and the plural gives two of them

explanation.surface: Lowering temperatures makes a tree hardy outside in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' removes both Ts from TOUGHENS TREE, and 'out' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass-walled building for growing plants or sitting among them is a glasshouse, much like a conservatory.

clue.text: Exposed area always reflected light source

indicators.note: reflected means turned back as in a mirror, so these letters read backwards

parts.note: ever means always
an LED, a light-emitting diode, is a source of light

explanation.surface: An exposed area constantly reflecting light, like a sunlit open patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflected' turns A and EVER round to make REVEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exposed has been uncovered or shown openly, brought into view.

clue.text: Dessert following starter of scallops

parts.note: following means coming after

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A pudding served after a starter of scallops, a restaurant meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' looks like the first course but takes S from 'scallops'. AFTERS is British slang for pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal word for the sweet course that comes after the main dish.
